utterances.text: He is the command structure, but on this sheet of paper it doesn't say "combat order," it doesn't say "order," it doesn't say "directive." It doesn't say anything. I would understand this as an instruction, as guidelines, yes. The military acts in accordance with with orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But this is certainly guidelines or instructions issued by a superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you send this kind of document to your subordinate units or clarification of these objectives and tasks, as it was said in this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We cannot take such instructions further down. Perhaps only to brigades, but not down to other units. This is explained at military meetings, briefings, meetings of the entire military personnel so that they would all be made aware of the policy of the government, or rather the state, or rather, the leadership of the JNA and the state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The question is simple. The soldiers under your command, were they aware of this? Did they know about this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to give the witness document P116, which is in tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, are you aware of the contents of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you personally receive such an order as commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes. There were several such orders or similar orders. I think I would have had to have received it. If the 2nd Operational Group received it, then I must have received it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise a thousand or 2.000 documents, but the substance, the content, tells me that I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This piece of paper in front of you, does it look like an authentic document of the chief of General Staff without a number and without a signature and with a preamble that is simple recounting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It could have been written as such any time, because it was not registered anywhere. It is not the type of document that is drafted in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you did receive this document, did you write an order of your own on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not write orders. Within combat orders and briefings, we familiarise personnel with specific matters that had to deal with this subject matter, but only in very concrete terms. That is what we told our subordinate men: Do not target the Old Town, do not target places of worship, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And which -- how did you transmit it to them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through orders, everyday combat orders were written; or during briefings, officers, commanders, were told about this. But of course not in such orders in writing. We did not do it that way. I did not get this paper, this document, from the 2nd Operational Group. I did not see it. So I could not have written any kind of order either. . If that's the answer you were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to give the witness a book.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May we know what excerpts or what the name of the book is? Prosecution is unaware of what is being presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to put the book on the ELMO. We just need to compare this book to a document that was a Prosecution exhibit, so we are not going to quote anything from this book. We are not going to read anything from this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, would you please compare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, what is the book, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to explain it now. This is a chronicle of documents from the field of defence of Yugoslavia 1990, 1991, the authors are Slavoljub Susic, Zlatoje Terzic, and Nikola Petrovic. I wanted to ask the witness to compare Prosecution Exhibit P116, which he had in his hands a few minutes ago, with page 469 of this book, which is a book of collected documents. So could it please be shown on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can a predicate be laid as to whether or not the witness is aware of the book, so that there's some basis for considering the evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I think we'll proceed with the book as it is for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just kindly ask that page 469 be placed on the ELMO and be zoomed in. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, the document that is a Prosecution exhibit, P116, that you had in your hands a few minutes ago and that we discussed, does it fully correspond to this page from the book, this page, 469, and 470? Are they identical? Or rather, is the Prosecution exhibit a copy of the two pages from this collection of documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see, yes, yes, from what I can see on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Look at the second page, too. Could you please compare it and say whether this Prosecution exhibit was copied from this book.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the book returned to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where does that leave us, Mr. Rodic? Either the book is a reliable publication setting out orders that were given, in which case the fact that we have a copy of the order from the book isn't of great significance; or the book is unreliable, and therefore this order is unreliable. Which are we to take to be the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the Defence is that the Defence -- actually, the Defence already presented its position during the examination-in-chief, when the Prosecutor introduced this document. The Defence did not object because we believed that the documents contained in this book were truthful. However, we wanted the Trial Chamber to know in this concrete case where this document came from and what its origin was. Because it is a very unusual document, as you could have seen from other documents tendered by the Prosecution. So according to its layout, it does not match authentic documents. But in terms of its content, it does constitute an authentic document. So the Defence does not object to the document, but we just wanted to identify where it came from. The Defence is going to use documents from this book for their case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are to treat it as a genuine order?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence, therefore, accepted this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, on page 2 of this order in paragraph 3 -- the second paragraph under item 3, actually, could you read it out and explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately submit a comprehensive report on any instance where opening fire on protected buildings could not have been avoided. Wherever possible, such cases should also be documented; photographs, video recordings, witness statements, and the like."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if there is an attack against a cultural landmark, if such an attack is carried out by the JNA, then this had to be reported? A report had to be submitted about it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And preferably, this report was supposed to be supported by photographs, video recordings, witness statements, et cetera. Did you have any knowledge by way of photographs or video recordings or witness statements, statements made by your officers, their soldiers, et cetera? Did you have any knowledge that such landmarks were fired at by way of a possible response?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could the question be asked within a time frame, please, Your Honour, so that it has some relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'm talking about the period between October and December 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards firing at places of worship and similar localities, I did not have any reports or recordings. But I do know of a few cases when I investigated how damage was incurred, as well as destruction -- the destruction of these monuments. I can mention only three cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The big old church in Cilipi, the church in Vitaljina, the village of Vitaljina, and the church at Gornji Brgat. The first one was damaged a very little bit. Also, it was broken into and some things were stolen from it. I personally toured it and ordered guards to be placed there. The second church was in Vitaljina. It was the bell tower that was damaged. However, that was before I came, and the explanation given to me was that there had been a machine-gun on the bell tower and that it had to be neutralised. The third case was that of the well-known church at Gornji Brgat. I think it is St. Anne's church. I'm not sure. Or the church of St. Lucas. It is -- it does not have a bell tower, but it has a kind of platform around it, and there was an artillery piece there. The 3rd Battalion considerably damaged or destroyed this section where the artillery piece was. I think that this church was shown in the Milosevic case. That's the only thing I know about religious buildings and their targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were informed about the fact that these facilities were used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the first case, but in the second two cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were you also informed that the Old Town is a protected site, was also abused in this manner; that is to say, used for military action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been such reports, mostly coming from the retired officers who became refugees, also from refugees themselves, also from lower ranking officers who fired upon certain areas and the Old Town itself. And there were also many reports in the press. It was suspected that within the vicinity of the walls of the old tower -- of the Old Town and the towers and about within 100 metres of them, there were weapons that were used for firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps watch any video depicting how there was firing coming from the Old Town and its walls?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of any video. I know that there was some artillery activity, but I didn't see any artillery activity from the Old Town depicted in a video. At least I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Your subordinate officers from military vessels, did they ever inform you whether they had been fired upon from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such reports coming from the vessels; they were normally sent via the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What did your subordinates tell you? Could you please tell us in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports quoted instances in which the vessels were fired upon by large-calibre guns, mortars, and other guns of smaller calibre. There were also instances in which anti-armour rounds were fired as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To clarify this, I asked you whether your subordinates located on ships reported to you that they had been fired upon, either from the walls, from the ramparts, or from within the Old Town itself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the early activity which took place in October in the vicinity of the town of Dubrovnik, also in early November, there were some reports that in the vicinity of walls and towers, especially on the side where the park of the Old City hospital was, as well as Bogosic park, there were some weapons firing towards Zarkovica and Dubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you told --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you told by subordinate officers on ships that there was any firing directed against them coming from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not from the Old Town. There was one report, as far as I can remember, that a 20-millimetre gun or something similar did fire; however, it was sporadic firing. As far as I can remember, there was just one such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This weapon was firing from what location?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Old Town, from the direction of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where was it positioned?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that there was a truck carrying 20-millimetre gun, either a one-barrelled or a double-barrelled gun. We knew that it changed its position moving about the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the ships respond to that fire? Did they report to you about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They reported to me that they did not respond to that fire because the fire was not dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you can remember, please tell me whether between October and November of 1991 -- October to December 1991 the subordinate officers on the ships ever reported to you that they had fired upon military targets in the Old Town, fired upon them or responded to their fire or anything similar.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never received such reports. There was no such activity taking place. There was firing directed against the area in the vicinity of the Old Town; against the hotels, again in the vicinity of the Old Town; but never against the Old Town itself. I never received such reports. And they wouldn't have dared report this to me, even if they had fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If they did not report this to you, did you yourself ever receive information that your ships fired upon the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only could have had suspected something like this at the time; however, after a rocket hit a ship and a commander and four sailors were injured, I stopped investigating that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify and give us more detail. Who fired at your ship with such a rocket?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two rockets were fired, one of them missed the target. It was a Maljutka-type rocket. The second one hit the command bridge on the ship, wounded four sailors and the ship's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what ship it was. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Patrol Boat 137. However, the rocket was not fired from the Old Town; but rather, from a small island called Olib or from its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where is this small island located?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north of Dubrovnik in the Kolocep canal quite a way from the Old Town or from Dubrovnik itself. However, there was some activity coming from the new town, which is a part of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you were able to establish that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Can we clarify that last sentence, please. It's unclear. The translation says: "There was activity coming from the new town, which is a part of the Old Town." I'm not sure -- I just have to ask if that was what was said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said: "Coming from the new town, which is outside of the Old Town."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So you meant parts of the town which are not considered parts of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please tell us whether you were able to establish that the Croatian forces had indeed Maljutka-type weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had Maljutka-type rockets. We seized three launchers in Dubac. They also had Ambrust launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain what these launchers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are German anti-armour rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this a convenient time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask the usher to provide the witness with P17, a document from tab 17 -- P117. Exhibit P117, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I wasn't able to see this report -- I couldn't have seen it, because it wasn't addressed to me or, rather, my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who was this report addressed to? Who is sending it and to whom is it being sent?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is being sent from the 1st Military District to the command of the Guards Motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The Guards Motorised Brigade, is it subordinated to the units of the command of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is subordinated to the 1st Military District, the Belgrade command in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a report of this kind at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But similar reports with this kind of content was expressed in combat orders, but I cannot be sure. However, that the Old Town specifically should not be targeted - and that is the essential point here - as well as places of worship, et cetera, those are basic things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecutor during the examination-in-chief, you said that you were aware of and knew of a report of this kind, this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said what I'm saying now. This was not addressed to me, to the guards brigade, and everything I said to you I repeated. But I said that similar contents were received probably by us, because I was aware of what we were allowed to do and what we weren't allowed to do, what was protected by various conventions and covenants and so on. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But a specific order or report of this kind you never saw?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's right. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to give P127, to be found in tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a report on the command of the 9th VPS sent to the command of the 2nd Operational Group with respect to the casualties, dead and wounded, from within your composition, your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It does refer to the 10th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at the names and dates when the soldiers were killed and the units to which they belonged, would it be correct that the largest number of casualties, dead, were from the 472nd Motorised Brigade on different days during October 1991? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The signature to this report by authorisation of the commander is Radovan Klikovac. Was he at the headquarters of the 9th VPS in the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an organisational and mobilisational officer, in charge of organisation and mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that means, what his tasks were and what his job was.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of organisation, the establishment of the unit, changes in organisation and establishment, and he also saw to the mobilisation of units within the 9th Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you explain that in a little more detail, please. When you say "mobilisation of units," what was his role and tasks within that sphere?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the plan for mobilisation and mobilisation classes and standard and orders for mobilisation, to all intents and purposes his job was to organise and compile all plans for orders for the unit's mobilisations, for his commander. And similarly, he takes part in mobilisation, together with the commanders of the corresponding units. He cooperates with municipalities and so on and so forth, or rather, with the organs from the municipalities which are in charge of mobilisation, which means the secretariats of defence of the Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does he in that way take part, or rather, organise the strength of the units, to see that there is a full complement?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is in charge of seeing to the strength of the units, to having a full complement as far as manpower is concerned and resources and materiel, especially looking at the lists for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us in what way a full complement of soldiers is secured for the units, or rather, what Lieutenant Colonel Klikovac was actually in charge of, what he was in charge of, how he manned the units, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to the manpower mobilised for the units is also -- also requires materiel and technical resources on the basis of lists compiled in the civilian sector of the sociopolitical communities and organisations, and labour organisations, work organisations. This would mean motor vehicles and other resources and materiel. There is a formation, an establishment, which in wartime has to be met and during peacetime training and exercises are conducted for mobilisation, where everything has to tally. The resources stipulated on lists have to tally with the resources on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- explain to us how you man your units, how you achieve a full complement. So instead of this very dry term "mobilisation," could you tell us what the role of Lieutenant Colonel Klikovac was in supplying the necessary soldiers, manpower, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't part of the mobilisation institution as such, but I'll do my best and tell you what I can, because I do know what is needed. On the basis of a mobilisation plan and mobilisation standards and the signals sent out for mobilisation, these signals are coded to individual commanders with all the requisites necessary and the Municipal Assemblies are apprised of that, which units are being mobilised, and each unit has a code assigned to it, unless we're dealing with a general mobilisation, which wasn't the case here. There was no proclamation of a general mobilisation, an all-out mobilisation. The organs in the municipalities themselves, based on the plans that they have, which are also coded, raise the necessary manpower, which went to provide the full strength of a unit, soldiers, reserve officers, et cetera, and resources and materiel on the basis of the compiled and supplied lists. The commander of the unit with his men, who have been charged with taking in the recruits mobilised in that way with a nucleus, an active nucleus, is what is formed. So they then take in the new men and materiel, and with that set up the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell me this, please: In cases of desertion, if anybody deserts from a unit, or if they fail to respond to the call-up for mobilisation, what happens then? The units will then have a problem of reaching a full complement of soldiers, won't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were a lot of problems in that respect because the response was meager, as far as I was able to gather from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that certain units needed specific men of specific training, specially trained men?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was a great deficiency and it was difficult to find men trained specifically for those units. This was difficult in peacetime, and it was even more difficult in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if the units did not have soldiers that were specially trained in the course of 1991, did you mobilise other people to those units who were not trained specifically for the specialty needed in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commanders, through necessity, had to accept those men that were sent to them, even if they hadn't been specifically and specially trained and who needed additional training to perform their duties. This was particularly important for certain units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which, give us an example of some of those units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 472nd Brigade, first and foremost. And then it applied to the 3rd Light Brigade, to a somewhat lesser extent, because the 3rd Brigade just had artillery weapons and a very weak supply of small arms. It had small arms but not enough of the other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, the artillery as a specialty, does it particularly require well-trained soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. With the artillery, this is most obvious, and the artillery needs specially trained soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Specifically dealing with the 472nd Brigade, in view of its strength by regular soldiers, recruits, and reservists, did they encounter that kind of problem?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It faced the most serious problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, was there an additional problem presented for units that were sent, soldiers that were not specifically trained, and was this aggravated by the general situation on the ground, which was tantamount to a situation of war because there were combat operations underway?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It made the situation all the more complex with requirements and demands being greatest for combat operations. So this was a highly complex situation, which called for specialised manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Faced with a situation where there was shooting and people being killed, was there any opportunity for training these untrained men, training them in a specialty of some kind? Could that have been done?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to ensure that under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this the kind of situation that reigned in the units of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, independently of the 2nd Operational Group at that time, that is to say during 1991, was that a general problem for the JNA because of the overall political situation in the country? Was that the problem the JNA had to face, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Certainly. And if I may be allowed to expand why these light infantry brigades were established in the first place. They had not previously been within their formation and establishmentwise, I wasn't aware of such units existing to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during that year of 1991, was there an open call from prominent individuals in political life and social life for military conscripts not to respond to the call-up from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember two or three cases from that time. One case was a brigade in Montenegro that was engaged in warfare in Banja. They were all asked to return and to abandon their positions in Banja. I know from amongst my own units from the territorial company of Mojkevac, when it threatened to leave its positions in line with the call issued to them by their president of their municipality. I also note that I think it was the Liberal Party that asked people to desert and not to respond to call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the case of the Valjevo unit, the Valjevo Brigade? Did it leave its positions, the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Valjevo Brigade was in the 37th Corps near Mostar. And except for some very small parts of it, it left its combat deployment in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness P123, which is in tab 31. P123, 123. It is in tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does this document constitute a proposal to normalise life in Dubrovnik and ensure the safety of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is this well-known proposal consisting of 11 points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this proposal was made by the JNA to Dubrovnik at that time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal was made by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik on the 26th of October, 1991, with a request for them to respond until the 27th of October, until 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So it's not in dispute that General Strugar is the signatory of these 11 points and this proposal in general. But can you explain then why VPS Boka is mentioned in this document and General Strugar is twice mentioned as the commander of VPS Boka.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time all information went through the sector command, that the 2nd Operational Group was not linked up in the communications system with Dubrovnik. So we were there only for transmission. We were a mere relay, so that's how this mistake took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So if I can put it this way, when mail goes from the 2nd Operational Group to the Crisis Staff and the monitoring mission of the European Community, it is sent through the command of the VPS Boka, because at that time it was possible for you to communicate with Dubrovnik better. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's the way it was. Although the 2nd Operational Group could use territorial links - but I don't know why they didn't - via the port of Bar and then the Dubrovnik harbour, but never mind now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and the other way around, from the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik and the monitoring mission, their mail and their messages, did they go to the VPS of Boka? And if they were addressed to General Strugar, were you supposed to send them then from Boka to Trebinje? Was that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't that kind of transmission. There were very frequent cases, and later on I think it was the rule as well, that the command in Trebinje directly received - I think by fax - the dispatches sent. I had the opportunity of seeing that, but at first it was like this, yes. But not all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the command in Kumbor or the forward command post in Kupari, the forward command post of the 9th VPS, in December 1991 did it have telephone communication with Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. The only thing we could do was from -- go from Kumbor to the port authority in Bar and then to the port of Dubrovnik. That was one way. And the second way was via Cavtat. Cavtat was the only one that still had a cable for communication with Dubrovnik. It just so happened that the cable was not destroyed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, where could a fax message be received from Dubrovnik vis-a-vis the VPS and the other way around, at which locality?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the signals people did it. I did not see these dispatches, as I said. Maybe it went through Kumbor. Perhaps there was a detached group of signals people from the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did the 9th VPS have its own signals people?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm saying is that it didn't go through me. That's what I wanted to say. These faxes did not go through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik or the monitoring mission of the European Community would send a message that would be received at the military naval sector, a message for General Strugar, and that it was then supposed to be sent on to him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it probably was that way. There certainly must have been such occasions, this being one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you talked about the port of Bar, I would like to know how this communication was established with Dubrovnik via Bar, by telephone? Radio link? Teleprinter? Or some other way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was radio communication and teleprinter communication. And fax?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, and did Dubrovnik, inter alia, communicate via Dubrovnik coastal radio?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When they went through Bar, was this also this coastal radio from Bar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's those communications, the coastal radio centres like Bar and Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned while giving evidence the 6th of December specifically and you said that you talked to Minister Davorin Rudolf, can you tell me how this communication was established, in which way.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian communications, wire communications, cable communications, over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: He telephoned you from Dubrovnik, and where were you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Cavtat. And possibly it was satellite telephone, as he claims. So he could not reach me in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever communicate with Dubrovnik from Kumbor over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, no. I don't know if I could have at all in wartime, because the wire transmission lines were destroyed. There was only a cable from Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness P134. It is in tab 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to this document -- or rather, does this come from the information service of the federal secretariat for national defence providing information on promotion of officers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Inter alia in this communication, Lieutenant Colonel General Pavle Strugar is mentioned who was given the rank of colonel general by a decree of the presidency of Yugoslavia dated the 28th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since this was a promotion that was beyond the regular line of promotions, whose duty was it to make such a proposal?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to regulations on promotions, it was supposed to be his superior officer. That is to say the chief of General Staff. He would propose to the presidency an extraordinary promotion to a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the presidency of the SFRY then, according to these regulations, it was in charge of promoting officers as far as these high ranks of general are concerned. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At that time in 1991, what was the 29th of November? Did that date mean something special then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of November was a national holiday. It was the day of the republic, the day when the republic had been established, the Republic of Yugoslavia, at that time the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the former SFRY, was that the prevalent practice, that on republic day decorations were awarded and on the occasion of that holiday officers were promoted to higher ranks in the military and also commendations, citations were handed out, too?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. I don't think so, because the 22nd of December was very soon after that, and that was the JNA Day when the military was promoted, awarded decorations, et cetera. The 29th of November was the day of the republic, but it was for different kinds of recognition. But we, the military, were not bound by that particular holiday. That was not the prevalent practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 29th of November was a state holiday, while the 22nd of December was just JNA Day. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is right, but extraordinary promotions are not linked to particular date. Extraordinary promotions are given because of the merits of the person who was promoted. It has to do with the particular event or a particular success achieved in that period when the promotion took place, but it's not linked to a particular date. It can be any date as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But don't you think that a state holiday, a national holiday -- the national holiday would be the right time for this kind of --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You seem to be trying to argue with the witness, Mr. Rodic, to get him to agree to something. He's already given you his understanding of the position. I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, why he was -- the officers stated here received extraordinary promotion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an explanation was given, always used to refer to senior officers for the successful management in command and for exceptional services and work in carrying out combat assignments of particular importance for the armed forces and the defence of the country. Specifically General Zivota Panic was promoted ahead of time because of the successful outcome to the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And do you know why General Strugar was nominated for promotion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assumed because he was successful in commanding the units of the Dubrovnik operation. For implementing the operational objectives that had been set in the blockade of Dubrovnik, in providing security for the Mostar airport, and achieving all the tasks and assignments that were given and specified in the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher's assistance again, please. Could he hand out the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a combat order by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to me and with orders to achieve certain objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether pursuant to these points the assignments were specifically enumerated, which would relate to the development of a naval blockade or assignments and tasks within a naval blockade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are specific assignments with regard to preventing navigation in the Kolocep canal and the introduction of weapons into Dubrovnik by speedboats and through maritime routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about point 4, does it give cautions and warnings with regard to the Old Town, that nobody should open fire on it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And it said that units exposed to enemy fire should withdraw. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, since your units were in charge of this part of the blockade from the sea, can you tell us what the main task and assignment of the units of the 9th VPS was at sea.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic task of the units, naval units at sea, was to effect a blockade of Dubrovnik and all the ports in the region of the Dubrovnik municipality from the sea and to prevent any vessels from sailing in, carrying weapons and other combat materiel, and to provide control for all loading and unloading and ship cargos, the cargos of ships given permission to sail into Dubrovnik harbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the basic aim of the blockade was to prevent weapons from being brought in to Dubrovnik by sea?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a decision that had been taken by the leadership of the JNA or the presidency, I'm not quite sure, on the basis of a resolution reached. I think the UN -- there was an UN resolution to prevent the import of weapons into Yugoslavia. And a blockade was ordered for all ports along the Adriatic coast, not only Dubrovnik ports but all the other ports along the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, did the units of the VPS perform their duties and tasks along the Adriatic coast as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The military district, not VPS. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they had to prevent the import of weapons along the Adriatic coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 69, line 22, it says "VPS" and it should read "VPO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The naval military -- military naval district. VPO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute or two more, Your Honour. With the Court's indulgence, if I may be allowed to take that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask one more question in this regard. So the objective of the blockade was to control the area and prevent any weapons from reaching Dubrovnik and the tasks that the units of the 9th VPS did. And apart from that, were vessels, ships, able to enter Dubrovnik with -- carrying people and food and other necessities after the vessels had been checked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although they weren't -- communication with Dubrovnik was not fully prevented and General Strugar was rather angry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since my time is up for the moment, Your Honour, could this document be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no question asked of the witness as to whether or not he in fact recognised this -- what purports to be an order or any predicate laid and I would just ask that perhaps we know whether this is something the witness knew of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the document is very clear, and clearly marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness, Mr. Rodic, or would you like me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can ask the witness, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document from the 1991 period? Did your command receive this document and were you aware of it and did you have knowledge of its contents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen the document and I do remember its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is marked D47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
